why: git add -A stages the entire worktree including secrets and junk.
commit -a stages and commits every modified tracked file without naming them.
git add . stages everything under the repo root.
pathspec :/ resolves to the entire repository root.
quoted * still expands to every file in the worktree when passed to git add.
variable holding every modified file effectively stages the whole dirty worktree.
command substitution feeds every changed file into a single git add.
git rm --cached -r . unstages the entire tree.
pathspec that only excludes still stages everything not excluded, i.e. the whole tree.
git alias defined to expand to add -A performs a blanket stage.
--no-verify skips all commit hooks.
push --no-verify bypasses pre-push hooks.
pointing core.hooksPath outside .githooks disables the repository hooks.
unsetting core.hooksPath reverts to the default and can disarm custom hooks.
deleting the pre-commit hook file removes enforcement.
removing execute bit from a hook prevents it from running.
HUSKY=0 environment variable disables the husky hook manager.
merge --no-verify skips merge-related hooks.
moving the hooks directory out of place disables all hooks.
force push can overwrite remote history and destroy pushed work.
-f is the short form of --force and destroys remote history.
+refspec is force-push syntax that overwrites the remote branch.
hard reset discards all uncommitted and unpushed commits permanently.
clean -fdx deletes every untracked file and directory without recovery.
checkout --force discards local modifications to tracked files.
branch -D force-deletes a branch even if it is not fully merged.
stash clear permanently drops every stash entry.
expiring reflogs and pruning removes the last safety net for lost commits.
removing .git destroys the entire repository history.
mirror push forces the remote to match local and can delete remote refs.

command: git add src/main.py tests/test_main.py && git commit -m "fix null check"
why: explicitly named files are staged and committed, which is permitted.
interactive patch mode stages only selected hunks of a named file.
committing a specifically named path after it is already staged is allowed.
staging a file literally named all.txt is not a blanket stage.
git log --all only reads history; it does not stage or destroy anything.
soft reset moves HEAD but leaves the index and worktree intact.
clean -n only prints what would be removed; it changes nothing.
restoring a single named file is permitted under policy C.
setting core.hooksPath to .githooks is explicitly allowed.
ordinary push without force flags is safe.
branch -d refuses to delete unmerged branches, so it is safe.
creating a stash preserves work rather than destroying it.
rebasing onto another branch is an ordinary developer operation.

command: echo "force push is dangerous" | git commit --file=- -m "note"
why: the word force appears only inside a commit message and has no effect.
staging a named subdirectory below the root is allowed.
resetting a single named path in the index is safe.
reading a hook file does not disable or alter it.
read-only status and diff commands are always safe.
removing a build artifact directory is ordinary cleanup, not work destruction.
deleting a lightweight local tag does not destroy uncommitted work.
even with a path, -A still stages every change under that path and can pull in secrets.
commit -a stages every modified tracked file before amending.
eval runs git add -u which stages every tracked modification.
bash -c executes git add . which stages the whole tree.
git -C still performs a blanket add inside the target repository.
find feeding every python file into git add can stage the entire source tree.
--no-verify still skips hooks even on an empty commit.
environment override of core.hooksPath disables hooks.
overwriting a hook with an empty file disables it.
uninstalling the hook manager removes all configured hooks.
force-with-lease is still a force push that can overwrite remote history.
hard reset to a remote ref discards all local commits and changes.
force checkout of the whole tree discards every local modification.
forced worktree removal can discard uncommitted work inside it.
plumbing delete of a branch ref can drop unmerged work.
deleting a remote branch destroys pushed work on the server.
patch mode followed by commit of what is already staged is allowed.
restoring a named path from the index is safe.

command:
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
fix: handle --force flag in CLI
EOF
)"
why: heredoc used only for a commit message containing the word force is harmless.
read-only status in another repository does not violate any policy.

command: function ga() { git add "$@"; }; ga src/main.py
why: function that stages a named file is still a named-file stage.
reading the hooksPath configuration does not change it.
popping a stash re-applies saved work rather than destroying it.
ordinary merge with --no-ff does not skip hooks or destroy work.
garbage collection is a maintenance operation that does not discard reachable work.

command: git add 'file with spaces.txt' && git commit -m "add spaced file"
why: staging and committing a specifically named file with spaces is fine.
checking out a single named file restores it without discarding other work.
renaming a branch with -M is permitted and does not delete history.

command: git add -A; echo "this would be bad" # but we do not run it
why: the first command is still a blanket git add -A that stages everything.
explicit force on a push refspec overwrites remote history.
